A reasonable reconciliation of these apparently different approaches and cases is that the communication must be part of a correspondence which the parties intend will reasonably lead to a compromise or settlement of the dispute. Hence, letters designed to open such negotiations, or letters or discussions which attempt to convince the opponent of the strengths of the other's position, but which also recognize weaknesses, in the hope that some settlement can be effected once each other's positions are on the table, should be subject to the privilege, whether or not they contain an actual offer of settlement. . . . . . There are a few exceptions to the rule that without prejudice correspondence may not be referred to in evidence. For example, if an application is brought to strike proceedings for want of prosecution, it is possible to explain the delay by indicating that negotiations have been underway. However, in these circumstances it will seldom be necessary or permissible to actually attach the without prejudice correspondence to an affidavit; it will be sufficient to merely refer to the discussions, and perhaps note the dates of the correspondence back and forth. There may also be statutory exceptions to this privilege, such as Rule 11. This Rule provides how long a statement of claim is in effect, how it can be reviewed, and the effects of expiry. Rule 11(9) provides when a defendant cannot rely on expiry of the statement of claim, and Rule 11(9)(a)(iii) includes as part of the test whether a person “purported to negotiate on behalf of the defendant.” This rule effectively makes negotiations a fact in issue. Therefore where Rule 11(9)(a)(iii) is relied on (i.e. a standstill agreement is alleged) it may be necessary to refer to correspondence that is clearly privileged. This should not be taken as a license by counsel to attach all manner of privileged correspondence to affidavits, even when a standstill agreement is alleged. In most cases an affidavit deposing to negotiations generally, and referring to correspondence back and forth, or perhaps quoting particular sentences, will be sufficient. In all cases actual sums offered should be blacked out; they are irrelevant and there is a risk they might come to the attention of the trial judge. Rule 173 prohibits reference to any formal offers. There is another situation that has nothing to do with settlement at all Correspondence is sometimes marked “without prejudice” other than when it is intended that the settlement privilege attach. For example, a lawyer might write outlining what he expects his client or another witness would say at trial. Comments such as this might be made as a form of disclosure, in order to simplify the proceedings. When they are marked “without prejudice,” that really means “this is not an admission.” Sometimes “without prejudice” is intended to preserve the formal rights of the party, or disclaim responsibility for the contents of the letter. Other examples are given by D. Vaver, “Without Prejudice Communications—Their Admissibility and Effect” (1974), 9 U.B.C. L. Rev. 85 at 164. Such correspondence is not generally admissible as evidence, not because it is privileged, but because it is hearsay, irrelevant or was not intended to have legal effect. In Leonardis v. Leonardis, 2003 ABQB 577, 2003 CarswellAlta 940, 50 Alta. L.R. (4th) 56, Slatter J. reaffirmed the statements he made in Hansraj v. Ao, 2002 ABQB 385, 2002 CarswellAlta 627, 314 A.R. 262, 4 Alta. L.R. (4th) 124; additional reasons at 2002 ABQB 772, 2002 CarswellAlta 1064, 314 A.R. 283, 4 Alta. L.R. (4th) 147; additional reasons at 2003 ABQB 299, 2003 CarswellAlta 508, 16 Alta. L.R. (4th) 296, and spoke specifically of the privilege which attaches to settlement correspondence. At p. 58, his Lordship said: This decision involves the third type of privilege, namely that relating to communications in furtherance of settlement. There are two important things to note about the settlement privilege. The first is that the privilege belongs to both parties, and it cannot be unilaterally waived by either one. Therefore, no party can unilaterally purport to waive privilege and attach such privileged materials to an affidavit or otherwise mention them in court. The second point is that it is the contents of the communication that determine if it is privileged, not the way it is labelled. If the contents of a communication are truly in furtherance of settlement and therefore privileged, it makes no difference whether the communication is marked “Without Prejudice” or not. A communication that is not in substance privileged does not become so just because one party places “Without Prejudice” on it. Likewise, the absence of the words “Without Prejudice” means nothing if the communication is truly privileged. … Slatter J. discussed the use of the phrase “With Prejudice”, and said at p. 60: There are occasions when it is appropriate to place “With Prejudice” on a letter. Examples are where the author of the letter seeks to fix legal rights, as where the letter demands payment of a sum, or exercises an option or election, or gives notice of a breach of a contract. However, placing “With Prejudice” on a settlement offer is inappropriate and ineffective. Justice Schutz in 1021018 Alberta Ltd. v. Bazinet, 2015 ABQB 151 explained how a Court should treat communications marked “with prejudice” (at paras 12-22) and applied Slatter J.'s decision in Leonardis v. Leonardis, 2003 ABQB 577, 2003 CarswellAlta 940, 50 Alta. L.R. (4th) 56. (xvi) Settlement negotiations It is, of course, well established that communications exchanged in the course of settlement negotiations often satisfy those criteria and accordingly are held to be privileged and inadmissible. . . . . . As Ruttan J. stated in Knight v. Ericksson (1958), 26 W.W.R. 203 at 204 (B.C. C.A.): “To permit evidence of offers made in such a manner to be used against the party making them would be to discourage parties from ever arriving at settlements to compromise litigation”. Costello v. Calgary (City) (1997), 53 Alta. L.R. (3d) 15 C.A., at pp. 45-46, per Picard J.A. In Bellatrix Exploration Ltd. v. Penn West Petroleum Ltd., 2013 ABCA 10, 2013 CarswellAlta 76, 542 A.R. 83, 81 Alta. L.R. (5th) 84, the Court gave this summary of the law of settlement privilege (at paragraphs 21–31): Purpose and Scope of Settlement Privilege 21 Settlement privilege is premised on the public policy goal of encouraging the settlement of disputes without the need to resort to litigation. It allows parties to freely discuss and offer terms of settlement in an attempt to reach a compromise. Because an admission of liability is often implicit as part of settlement negotiations, the rule ensures that communications made in the course of settlement negotiations are generally not admitted into evidence. Otherwise, parties would rarely, if ever, enter into settlement negotiations to resolve their legal disputes. 22 Other justifications for the rule have been offered, including the notion that an implied contract is created between negotiating parties, such that any admissions made in their discussions will be considered confidential. While this theory has often been rejected as being problematic and not well-founded, it has received some recent acceptance in the English case law, which was expanded upon by the Newfoundland Court of Appeal in Meyers. 23 Alberta courts have adopted the public policy rationale for the rule: see Ed Miller Sales & Rentals Ltd v. Caterpillar Tractor Co. (1990), 105 AR 4, 72 Alta LR (2d) 330, aff'd 74 Alta LR (2d) 271, [1990] 5 WWR 377 (CA). See also Costello at para 94; Hansraj v. Ao, 2002 ABQB 385, 314 AR 262, rev'd on other grounds 2004 ABCA 223, 354 AR 91. This approach is consistent with the underlying objective that the parties should be permitted to freely “put all their cards on the table” without having to worry that they may be prejudiced should negotiations fail to resolve their dispute. 24 Courts appear to have accepted that the types of communications covered by the settlement privilege require at least a hint of potential compromise or negotiation: see, for example, Hansraj at para 20. However, an unconditional assertion of rights without any connection to the possibility of settlement or negotiation do not fall within the scope of the rule: Buckinghamshire County Council v. Moran, [1990] 1 Ch 623, [1989] 3 All ER 225 (CA), cited in Hansraj at para 19. Communications of this type do not offer any potential for compromise, which is the interest the privilege is intended to protect. 25 The notation “without prejudice” is not conclusive in establishing privilege. If the contents of a communication are truly in furtherance of settlement, and therefore privileged, it makes no difference whether the communication is marked “without prejudice” or not. A communication that is not in substance privileged does not become so just because one party places “without prejudice” on it. Likewise, the absence of the words “without prejudice” means nothing if the communication is truly privileged: see Leonardis v. Leonardis, 2003 ABQB 577 at para 6, 50 Alta LR (4th) 56; Phillips v. Rogers (1988), 92 AR 253, 62 Alta LR (2d) 140 (QB); William Allan Real Estate Co v. Robichaud (1987), 37 BLR 286, 17 CPC (2d) 138 (Ont HC); Underwood v. Cox (1912), 21 OWR 757, 26 OLR 303 at 310 (Div Ct); Imperial Oil Ltd. v. 416169 Alberta Inc., 2002 ABQB 386 at para 30, 310 AR 338. 26 As settlement privilege operates to preclude admission of evidence that might otherwise be relevant, it competes with the court's truth-seeking function. For that reason, courts must ensure the communications come within the tripartite test before applying the privilege. However, once that test is met, the privilege must be given broad scope and attach not only to communications involving offers of settlement but also to communications that are reasonably connected to the parties' negotiations. The privilege belongs to both parties and cannot be unilaterally waived or overridden by either of them: see Hansraj at para 13. 27 It is to be remembered that the rationale for the privilege is not limited to the notion that it would be unfair to subsequently prejudice one of the parties by admitting any admissions made during settlement negotiations. The rule is also intended to allow parties to freely and openly discuss the potential for a settlement, and while doing so, the parties should not have to carefully monitor the content of their discussions. As noted by Lord Walker in Unilever plc v. The Procter & Gamble Co. (1999), [2001] 1 All ER 783 at para 35, [2000] 1 WLR 2436 (CA): the protection of admissions against interest is the most important practical effect of the rule. But to dissect out identifiable admissions and withhold protection from the rest of without prejudice communications (except for a special reason) would not only create huge practical difficulties but would be contrary to the underlying objective of giving protection to the parties. 28 In other words, the rule's protection is not meant to be limited to the prejudice that an admission may have at trial specifically, but on the potential impairment on settlement discussions as an important element of the litigation process generally. Accordingly, for the rule to operate properly, not only must the ambit of the settlement privilege be broad, but the exceptions to the exclusionary rule must be narrowly construed and only be given effect where another policy objective can be shown to outweigh any impact that may arise to the settlement objective. Exceptions to Settlement Privilege 29 As with most forms of privilege, there are exceptions to the rule. Some are universally accepted, while others are more controversial. Among the generally recognized exceptions are the following: (a) to prevent double recovery: Dos Santos (Committee of) v. Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada, 2005 BCCA 4, 207 BCAC 54; (b) where the communications are unlawful, containing for example, threats or fraud; (c) to prove that a settlement (an accord and satisfaction) was reached, or to determine the exact terms of the settlement: Comrie v. Comrie, 2001 SKCA 33, 203 Sask R 164; (d) it is possible that the settlement posture of the parties can be relevant to costs. That is clearly the case with offers made under the Rules of Court, but also with respect to informal offers: Mahe v. Boulianne, 2010 ABCA 74 at paras 8–10, 21 Alta LR (5th) 277; Calderbank v. Calderbank, [1975] 3 All ER 333 (CA). 30 Some of these may not truly be exceptions to the rule, but simply matters outside the scope of the rule. For example, using without prejudice communications to prove that a settlement was actually achieved is not inconsistent with the policy behind the privilege. Similarly, it may be that even if part of a communication is covered by the privilege another part, such as a separate enclosure might not be. 31 The English cases identify some possible exceptions to the privilege, sometimes in very wide terms. For example, Lord Walker stated in Unilever at para 37: “… the veil imposed by public policy may have to be pulled aside, even so as to disclose admissions, in cases where the protection afforded by the rule has been unequivocally abused.”[emphasis added.] However, courts must proceed cautiously before establishing exceptions to settlement privilege, as the underlying public policy justification is a compelling one: see Brown v. Cape Breton (Regional Municipality), 2011 NSCA 32 at para 65, 331 DLR (4th) 307. At paragraph 34, the Court added: 34 It must be remembered that the settlement privilege is an established “class” privilege. It is recognized in law, and does not have to be justified each time under the Wigmore test: Brown at paras 50–61. In addition to creating great uncertainty, the approach suggested by the Master would convert the privilege from a class privilege to a case-by-case privilege. Settlement discussions cannot proceed with the necessary candour if the parties can never be sure if a judge will later decide it is “not fair” to recognize the privilege. Bellatrix Exploration Ltd. v. Penn West Petroleum Ltd., 2013 ABCA 10, 2013 CarswellAlta 76, 542 A.R. 83, 81 Alta. L.R. (5th) 84, was quoted with approval in Phoa v. Ley, 2020 ABCA 195, 2020 CarswellAlta 894, 9 Alta. L.R. (7th) 1. In Borgel v. Paintearth (Subdivision and Development Appeal Board), 2020 ABCA 321, 2020 CarswellAlta 1629, 4 M.P.L.R. (6th) 11, the appellants were successful in their appeal of a subdivision and development appeal board (SDAB) order, and subsequently sought costs as against both the SDAB and the County. The County made an offer to settle costs, and the offer was made “on a with prejudice basis”. That offer was not accepted. In discussing the “with prejudice” offer, the Court of Appeal said: [19]… We interpret the County's emphasis on the expression “with prejudice” in each offer as putting the appellants on notice that whether or not these discussions were negotiations of a sort, they were not subject to a privilege claim. Express deployment of the phrase “without prejudice” does not necessarily achieve privilege on everything putatively covered by the expression: compare Bellatrix Exploration Ltd. v Penn West Petroleum Ltd., 2013 ABCA 10 at para 25, 358 DLR (4th) 628; Union Carbide Canada Inc. v Bombardier Inc., 2014 SCC 35, at para 34, [2014] 1 SCR 800 [20] That said, the language chosen by the County certainly puts paid to any suggestion that privilege applied when the County made its position blatant that it did not intend its communications to be privileged. Moreover, privilege applies to negotiations as to the substantive issue: see Bellatrix; Union Carbide; Sable Offshore Energy Inc. v. Ameron International Corp., 2013 SCC 37, [2013] 2 SCR 623; Ofulue v Bossert, [2009] UKHL 16, [2009] 3 All ER 93 (which contains extensive discussion of the “without prejudice” doctrine and its foundation and exceptions); Oceanbulk Shipping & Trading SA v TMT Asia Limited, [2010] UKSC 44, [2010] 4 All ER 1011. The question whether the privilege applies to discussions about costs is for another day; it has been said that the revelation of privileged discussions may be necessary to explain a settlement or may itself be relevant itself to costs: see Ofulue at para 23 per Lord Hope. [21] In any event, for the County to expressly disclaim privilege at the outset speaks for itself. It should not undermine the wider policy of encouraging settlement by way of giving the cover of privilege to confidential negotiations to settle for a party to disclaim privilege: compare Union Carbide at paras 31–34; Ofulue at paras 32–36, 58, 98-99. In Ed Miller Sales & Rentals Ltd. v. Caterpillar Tractor Co. (1990), 72 Alta. L.R. (2d) 330 (Q.B.); [affirmed (1990) 74 Alta. L.R. (2d) 271 (C.A.)], Wachowich J. (as he then was) had before him the following issue: “whether a stranger to unsuccessful ‘without prejudice’ negotiations for settlement of an action is entitled, on discovery, to examine a party to the negotiations on the content of the discussions.” In dismissing the application for an order directing that questions about the negotiations be answered, his Lordship said, at pp. 332-33: Four rationales for the “without prejudice” rule have been endorsed by various authorities. The first, propounded by Professor Wigmore, interprets the rule as a reflection of the fact that a party's willingness to compromise or settle a claim is not necessarily grounded in the belief that the claim is well founded … The communications are, therefore, excluded as irrelevant, failing to support an inference of admitted liability. Second, it has been suggested that the courts should not lend their approval to one party prejudicing and opponent by using admissions made by an opponent during bona fide efforts aimed at settling the action … Third, the inability to compel discovery on or adduce evidence of admissions made during negotiations for compromise has been said to be founded on an express or implied agreement between the parties … Finally, the fourth rationale for the “without prejudice” doctrine is public policy. It has been held that parties should be encouraged to settle their disputes without litigation; to expose admissions made during negotiations for settlement would undermine this policy objective … Wachowich J. then concluded at p. 338: … I am of the view that the better position in law is that a stranger to “without prejudice” negotiations for settlement is not entitled to disclosure of the content of such discussions during examination for discovery in the circumstances of this case. In Western Canadian Place Ltd. v. Con-Force Products Ltd. (1998), 233 A.R. 180 (Q.B.), McMahon J. had before him an application to compel disclosure of a settlement agreement to a stranger. This case differed from Ed Miller Sales & Rentals Ltd. v. Caterpillar Tractor Co. (1990), 72 Alta. L.R. (2d) 330 (Q.B.); [affirmed (1990) 74 Alta. L.R. (2d) 271 (C.A.)], which dealt with failed settlement negotiations. At pp. 183-84, McMahon J. said: In the critical task of balancing the two different public interests, namely the public interest in promoting settlements and the public interest in full discovery between parties to litigation, I have no doubt that the documents and contents of negotiations leading up to a settlement remain privileged notwithstanding that a settlement is reached. . . . . . To weigh the competing interests I conclude that a concluded agreement, assuming relevance, cannot remain privileged. Either party to it may sue upon it. It may affect the rights and interests of others—for example on the issue of damages and values. The weight to be given to it is another matter entirely and is for the trial judge. The policy objective of encouraging settlement has been achieved. Now the primary interest is in full disclosure of relevant documents. 35 Bellatrix argues that Penn West has not met the requirements of the test. (xvii) Chain e-mails In Alberta (Municipal Affairs) v. Alberta (Information and Privacy Commissioner), 2019 ABQB 274, 2019 CarswellAlta 704, 92 Alta. L.R. (6th) 191, Justice Mandziuk reviewed documents for which privilege had been claimed. Some of the documents formed an “e-mail chain”, parts of which were not directly between a lawyer and another person. His Lordship discussed how to deal with such chains: [13] Broadly speaking, the Sealed Records consist of: a) Emails and executive summaries disseminated among members of the internal government client groups or departments that relay or exchange information about ongoing arbitration proceedings and/or advice about arbitrations, experts, legal strategy and related matters with legal counsel included in the email string. b) Emails exchanged between legal counsel, and between legal counsel and their client groups or departments, providing legal advice, sharing information and making inquiries related to providing legal advice. c) Briefing notes and analogous reports with legal counsel input concerning arbitration and legal proceedings and otherwise referencing legal advice and opinion. d) Correspondence between internal legal counsel and legal counsel for arbitration parties. [14] On my review, and examination of each document or group of like documents, I find that the contents of the Sealed Records are privileged: Suncor at paras 29, 35. [15] The documents reviewed do not fall into the category of “policy advice,” as I found them to be distinguishable from communications that might be so classified: Pritchard at paras 19-20. [16] Many of the emails are expressly labelled as “privileged and confidential” or have words to that effect contained in them. In those instances, their substance is consistent with their characterization. [17] There are emails in “chains” that are not directly between lawyer and client, or lawyer and lawyer, but have been sent by and received from members of the client group or department. Communications in this category request and give information, make inquiries, answer questions and otherwise relate topically to those in which legal counsel are directly involved. [18] Those emails form part of a discrete body of communications that includes clearly privileged material. I must take a holistic approach to this question. In these instances, they are “part of a continuum in which legal advice is given”: Calgary (Police Service) at para 6. What all of them have in common is that they essentially “transmit or comment” on the work products that, I find, are privileged: Bank of Montreal v Tortora, 2010 BCSC 1430 (CanLII) at paras 11-12, 14 BCLR (5th) 386. [19] The case law guides me to take a broad and contextual view of solicitor-client privilege in assessing the Sealed Records. The legal principles that inform my reasoning in the present case include the following: a) “The legal advice privilege protects all communications, written or oral, between a solicitor and a client that are directly related to the seeking, formulating or giving of legal advice; it is not necessary that the communication specifically request or offer advice, as long as it can be placed within the continuum of communication in which the solicitor tenders advice; it is not confined to telling the client the law and it includes advice as to what should be done in the relevant legal context”: Samson Indian Nation and Band v Canada, 1995 CanLII 3602 (FCA), [1995] 2 FC 762 at para 8, 1125 DLR (4th) 294 (FCA) (WL). b) As far back as 1979, the Supreme Court of Canada confirmed that “there is no question that the Canadian courts have been moving towards a broader concept of solicitor-client privilege”: Solosky v The Queen, 1979 CanLII 9 (SCC), [1980] 1 SCR 821 at para 26, 105 DLR (3d) 745. c) Solicitor-client privilege is not “limited merely to the initial recipient of the solicitor's legal advice and opinion”: Bank of Montreal at para 11; d) “The privilege will extend to documents between employees which transmit or comment on privileged communications with lawyers. The privilege will also extend to include communications between employees advising of communications from lawyer to client”: Bank of Montreal at para 12; citing Mutual Life Assurance Co of Canada v Canada (Deputy Attorney General), [1988] OJ No 1090, 28 CPC (2d) 101 (Ont SCJ). [20] There is jurisprudence concerning third-party communications that is of some assistance, analogically and theoretically, in this case particularly as it pertains to this question of continuum. [21] In General Accident Assurance Co v Chrusz (1999), 1999 CanLII 7320 (ON CA), 124 OAC 356 at paras 88–98, 180 DLR (4th) 241 (Ont CA), the Ontario Court of Appeal addressed the issue of whether or not communications between legal counsel and an adjuster, both retained by the insurer, were protected by solicitor- client privilege. The approach set out in General Accident Assurance has been described as a “functional analysis,” under which “the court must determine whether the third-party communications are in furtherance of a function which is essential to the existence or operation of a relationship between the solicitor and the client”: Bank of Montreal at para 18. [22] In general, one can take from General Accident Assurance that the determination of solicitor-client privilege is contextual, fact based and evidence-dependent and the criteria for the existence of privilege is the necessary pre-condition for all determinations, including those that arise from third-party involvement. [23] In British Columbia (Attorney General) v Lee, 2017 BCCA 219 (CanLII) at para 50, 414 DLR (4th) 635, Hunter JA of the British Columbia Court of Appeal held that the email string of communications that encompassed “the discussion by staff and the adjudicator of the solicitor's advice, the day after the followup advice was received,” constituted in his opinion “part of the continuum of communications that is protected by the privilege […] To permit disclosure of this email exchange would disclose the legal advice itself and accordingly cannot be severed from the protected whole.” [24] Also, in New Brunswick v Enbridge Gas New Brunswick Limited Partnership, 2016 NBCA 17 (CanLII) at para 19, 447 NBR (2d) 201, the New Brunswick Court of Appeal observed “there is an ‘expansive’ modern Canadian view that solicitor-client privilege attaches to all communications in the ‘continuum of communications’ which applies to the normal functioning of government,” citing Adam M Dodek, Solicitor-Client Privilege, (Markham: LexisNexis Canada Inc, 2014) at Chapter 12. [25] Consequently, and in the context of Gill J's February 13, 2019 Consent Procedural Order, I find that solicitor-client privilege attaches to all of the documents contained in the Sealed Records. I have reviewed them individually. (xviii) Continuum of communication In Power v. RGMP, 2021 ABQB 877, 2021 CarswellAlta 2819, Justice Grosse gave this summary: [16] Solicitor-client privilege is not merely a rule of evidence. It is recognized as a fundamental principle of substance, as close to absolute as possible: R v McClure, 2001 SCC 14 at paras 2, 5 and 35. In order for a communication to be protected by solicitor-client privilege, it must: (a) Be made between a lawyer and a client; (b) Entail seeking or providing legal advice; and (c) Be intended by the lawyer and client to be confidential. Canada v Solosky, 1979 CanLII 9 (SCC), [1980] 1 SCR 821 at 837. [17] Although not all communications between legal counsel and a client are privileged, the Court does not engage in a line by line review to identify “advice”. A “continuum of communications” between lawyer and client is necessary in order for the lawyer to understand the client's circumstances and advise accordingly. Communications are protected if they fall within that continuum, even if that particular communication does not itself specifically include advice or a request for advice: Blood Tribe v Canada (Attorney General), 2010 ABCA 112 at para 26. This is consistent with one of the underlying premises of solicitor-client privilege, being the need for clients and lawyers to be able to communicate freely and candidly: McClure at para 2. Undue parsing would thwart this objective. Where a corporation is the client, communications within the corporation for the purposes of discussing a request for advice, or advice received, or otherwise to obtain advice and instruct counsel, may be subject to solicitor-client privilege: Bank of Montreal v Tortora, 2010 BCSC 1430 at para 12. [18] Whether a particular communication is privileged is contextual and must be decided based on the evidence in the case before the court: General Accident Assurance Co v Chrusz, 1999 CanLII 7320 (ON CA), 1999 CarswellOnt 2898 at paras 95-96, per Doherty JA, dissenting on other points. The party asserting a privilege bears the onus of establishing the privilege: Alberta (Provincial Treasurer) v Pocklington Foods Inc, 1993 ABCA 69; 1993 CarswellAlta 312 at para 42. The Court may infer that some elements of the test are met, without specific evidence: Blood Tribe at para 19. For example, if a communication is clearly between a lawyer and client for the purpose of giving or receiving legal advice, and there is no evidence that it was shared with any third party, an inference is readily available that the communication was intended to be confidential. C. — Common Interest Privilege [19] Many of the records in dispute are not communications between one party and their counsel. Rather, they are communications between CanAm and RGMP, or between their respective transaction counsel, or some combination of parties and counsel. In cases where the communication is not between counsel and client, CanAm and RGMP argue that the records are subject to “common interest privilege”. They describe the communications as being “in furtherance of the transaction” or “for the purposes of completing the offering” or similar descriptions. [20]“Common interest privilege” is not a stand-alone privilege. Common interest privilege only protects records that are otherwise protected by another privilege. In fact, it is frequently suggested that common interest privilege is not a privilege at all, but rather, an exception to the doctrine of waiver: Piney Bowes of Canada Ltd v R, 2003 FTC 214 at para 14; A Dodek, Solicitor-Client Privilege (LexisNexis Canada Inc, 2014) at § 7.162. Because confidentiality is an essential element of solicitor-client privilege, if a party knowingly shares communication that would otherwise meet the test for solicitor-client privilege with a third party, the privilege is often waived: see the summary of waiver in Dodek, supra at § 7.4. Common interest privilege acknowledges that in some circumstances, the holder of the privilege and the third party may have sufficient common interest in the subject matter of the privileged communication, including an interest in maintaining confidence, that disclosure to the third party does not interfere with the communication's privileged status. [21]“Common interest privilege” was originally recognized in the context of parties with a common interest in the subject matter of anticipated litigation sharing advice or documents: Buttes Gas and Oil Co v Hammer (No 3), [1980] All ER 475 (Eng CA), varied [1982] AC 888 (HL). It has been applied to both communication subject to solicitor-client privilege and to information subject to litigation privilege. For the purposes of this decision, I need not address the distinctions between those two privileges and their underpinnings, and how those distinctions impact the application of “common interest privilege”: see Pinder v Sproule, 2003 ABQB 33 at paras 54, 62. It is important that a party claiming “common interest privilege” articulate the basis on which the record is privileged and how the “common interest privilege” applies to that particular record. [22] I note at this juncture that common interest privilege is not to be confused with joint client privilege. The latter applies where two parties retain the same counsel, or in other circumstances where the advice is deemed to be sought for the joint benefit of more than one party: Dodek, supra at § 2.4. There is no claim of joint client privilege here. [23] Common interest privilege has now expanded beyond the context of litigation or anticipated litigation. Canadian law recognizes that parties to a transaction may enjoy common interest privilege.[2] In Iggillis Holdings Inc v Canada (Minister of National Revenue), the Federal Court of Appeal described common interest privilege in the transaction context as follows: “… solicitor-client privilege is not waived when an opinion provided by a lawyer to one party is disclosed, on a confidential basis, to other parties with sufficient common interest in the same transactions”: Iggillis Holdings Inc v Canada (Minister of National Revenue), 2018 FCA 51 at para 41; leave to appeal dismissed [2018] SCCA No 207 (QL). [24] Most of the commonly cited cases on common interest privilege in a transaction context involve substantive legal opinions shared by parties to a transaction, often on a specific legal point, such as foreign law or tax: for example, see Archean Energy Ltd v Minister of National Revenue, 1997 CarswellAlta 247 at para 30; Fraser Milner Casgrain LLP v Minister of National Resources, 2002 BCSC 1344; Pitney Bowes of Canada Ltd v R, 2003 FCT 214; Iggillis, supra. Another confirmed example is disclosure of privileged records so as to permit the counterparty to do due diligence on the underlying subject matter: Anderson Exploration Ltd v Pan-Alberta Gas Ltd, 1998 ABQB 455. … [35] In considering the application of solicitor-client privilege and common interest privilege in this context, I see a distinction between a party conveying a position, or making a request or demand of the other party, and sharing legal advice. To take a general example, not at issue in this particular case, counsel may provide advice to a client that a certain form of indemnity would be in the client's best interest. Such advice is prima facie subject to solicitor-client privilege. However, if the client accepts that advice, and, in the course of negotiations with the counterparty, requests the inclusion of that indemnity, the request to the counter-party is not likely to be treated as sharing solicitor-client privileged information. The same is true whether the request for the indemnity is conveyed by the client or by counsel. Without more, the request for the indemnity is more akin to a statement of position, or a volley in the negotiations, than to a sharing of privileged legal advice. If all such communications were protected under the umbrella of solicitor-client privilege and common interest privilege, just because they were based on legal advice, or because counsel was involved in the communication, it would amount, in effect, to the creation of a stand-alone transactional privilege for any deals involving counsel. No such privilege has ever been recognized. CanAm and RGMP do not expressly argue for any such recognition, but it would be the natural extension of their position. [36] Of course, the line may not always be clear, and each case turns on its own facts and record. A series of similar communication could be found to be privileged in one case, and not in another, either because of differing surrounding circumstances, different specific content, different specificity of evidence before the court, or a myriad of other factors. My reasons herein should not be taken as trying to draw hard and fast rules about certain types of records or patterns of communications in the context of every commercial transaction. [37] General descriptions of types of records that I have concluded are not privileged in the Production Application include: • Emails between counsel requesting or providing status updates. • Emails directly between counsel for one party and representatives of the other party requesting or providing factual information. • Communications between the parties discussing tasks to be completed and requesting or providing factual information. Similarly, privilege may be set aside when the safety of the public is at risk from nondisclosure of the communications: Jones v. Smith, [1999] 1 S.C.R. 455, 236 N.R. 201, 120 B.C.A.C. 161, 196 W.A.C. 161. In addition, the continued existence of solicitor-client privilege is not required where the client no longer has an interest to protect and where nondisclosure would compromise the ability of an accused to defend himself: Smith. Finally, while the duty of confidentiality survives the death of the client, the privilege enures to the client's successor in title (e.g., heirs) and may be waived by a successor in interest to the client: Goodman Estate v. Geffen, [1991] 2 S.C.R. 353, 127 N.R. 241, 125 A.R. 81, 14 W.A.C. 81, 81 D.L.R. (4th) 211, [1991] 5 W.W.R. 389, 80 Alta. L.R. (2d) 293, 42 E.T.R. 97 at p. 384 [S.C.R.]. Bre-X Minerals Ltd. (Bankrupt), Re (2001), 293 A.R. 73 (C.A.), at 81, per Conrad J.A. (xxii) A trustee in bankruptcy may not waive bankrupt's privilege In Bre-X Minerals Ltd. (Bankrupt), Re, 2001 ABCA 255, 2001 CarswellAlta 1363, 293 A.R. 73, 97 Alta. L.R. (3d) 1, Conrad J.A. held that the trustee in bankruptcy does not, by virtue of being the trustee, acquire rights over solicitor-client privilege belonging to the bankrupt. At pp. 81-82, Her Ladyship said: Solicitor-client privilege is the privilege of the client—in this case, Bre-X. Subject to an exception, the only basis upon which a trustee could claim the right or power to waive the bankrupt's solicitor-client privilege and demand disclosure would be statutory. It is important to understand the powers of a trustee when resolving the question of privilege. A trustee has no inherent authority over the bankrupt's affairs. Rather, the trustee's rights are statutory and it is empowered to assume conduct of the bankrupt's affairs and take possession of his property pursuant to authority granted by the [Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act]. … At p. 86, she concluded: In my view, there is no attempt in the legislation to displace the common law confidentiality rights enjoyed by a bankrupt with respect to its communications with solicitors. The privilege itself is not property under the [Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act]. Nor is the right to waive a power attaching to property divisible amongst creditors under s. 67. The essence of the privilege, whatever its form, is the confidential communication to which privilege attaches. An explicit delegation would be required in order for trustees to have a categorical right to waive privilege for bankrupts and even for trustees to have an enhanced ability to seek the authority to waive from the courts on a case-by-case basis. Thus, the personal right of privilege is not altered by the [Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act]. (xxiii) The effect of allegations of fraud In Yawrenko v. Boyle (1999), 256 A.R. 115 (Q.B.), a claim of civil fraud was made against the defendants. The plaintiffs applied for an order compelling solicitors who advised the defendants to produce their files. In dismissing the application, Clarke, J. said, at pp. 118-119: The law in Alberta can be found in the case of 383618 Alberta Ltd. v. National Quick-Freeze & Produce Ltd. et al., [1995] A.J. No. 1337 (Q.B. Master) (Master Funduk), at para. 5 and para. 6 he says: In this action the plaintiff says that what National did were fraudulent transactions designed to defeat its creditors. In their defence the defendants deny that the transactions were fraudulent. They plead that they were ‘bona fide transactions’. He then goes on to adopt as the law in Alberta a decision of the B.C. Court of Appeal at para. 15 as follows: Pax Management Ltd. v. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, [1987] 5 W.W.R. 252 (B.C. C.A.), discusses the denial of a solicitor-client privilege where fraud is a legitimate issue in the action, pp. 260-261: … Be that as it may, to accede to the plaintiffs, submission on the facts of this case might well establish a practice that wherever there is a claim framed in fraud and affidavit material is filed supporting the relevance of the communications to the issue raised in the pleadings, the client would be denied this long-established and important privilege. Kekewich, J., recognized this dichotomy in this passage from Williams v. Quebrada Ry., Land & Copper Co., supra, at p. 754: This case is, in my opinion, one of unusual gravity and importance. It is of the highest importance, in the first place, that the rule as to privilege of protection from an expectant or possible litigant, and his solicitor should not be in any way departed from. However hardly the rule may operate in some cases, long experience has shewn that it is essential to the due administration of justice that the privilege should be upheld. On the other hand, where there is anything of an underhand nature or approaching to fraud, especially in commercial matters, where there should be the veriest good faith, the whole transaction should be ripped up and disclosed in all its nakedness to the light of the court. The denial of privilege in such circumstance is not based on waiver by the client, express or implied, but simply on the policy basis that the benefits of maintaining the privilege are outweighed by the benefits to be derived, in cases where fraud is a genuine issue, from full disclosure of all circumstances relevant to resolving that issue including those circumstances contained in documents which are usually protected from disclosure by reason of the solicitor-client privilege. Viscount Finlay in O'Rourke v. Darbishire, [1920] A.C. 581 at 604 (H.L.), set out what I respectfully consider to be required of the applicant in order to displace the solicitor-client privilege: If the communications to the solicitor were for the purpose of obtaining professional advice, there must be, in order to get rid of privilege, not merely an allegation that they were made for the purpose of getting advice for the commission of a fraud, but there must be something to give colour to the charge. The statement must be made in clear and definite terms, and there must further be some prima facie evidence that it has some foundation in fact. It is with reference to cases of this kind that it can be correctly said that the court has a discretion as to ordering inspection of documents. It is obvious that it would be absurd to say that the privilege could be got rid of merely by making a charge of fraud. The court will exercise its discretion, not merely as to the terms in which the allegation is made, but also as to the surrounding circumstances, for the purpose of seeing whether the charge is made honestly and with sufficient probability of its truth to make it right to disallow the privilege of professional communications. I have concluded that the plaintiffs have specifically pleaded fraudulent misrepresentation and that the surrounding circumstances, as revealed by the affidavits filed in support of the application, satisfy me that the claim is honestly advanced and has sufficient credence to justify exercising the court's discretion to disallow the privilege so that all relevant material is before the court when resolving this very serious allegation. Accordingly, I direct that the defendant bank produce to the plaintiffs the correspondence between it and its solicitors, Davis & Company, which is set out at tabs 14 to 21 inclusive of the book of documents provided for this court's inspection. … From these cases I have concluded that that merely making a charge of fraud is not enough. The court is required to review the surrounding circumstances for the purpose of seeing whether the charge is made honestly and with sufficient probability of its truth to make it right to disallow the privilege of professional communications. Put another way, there must be some prima facie evidence that fraud has some foundation in fact. (xxiv) Bad faith claims In Sovereign General Insurance Co. v. Tanar Industries Ltd., 2002 ABQB 101, 2002 CarswellAlta 83, 316 A.R. 212, 98 Alta. L.R. (3d) 88, litigation arose out of the construction of a power plant. Sovereign General Insurance paid out the claims of certain subcontractors, and then claimed against a labour and material payment bond issued by American Home Assurance Company. American Home retained legal counsel to investigate and defend the claim. The Sovereign Insurance claim included an allegation of bad faith on the part of American Home, which American Home denied. One of the issues to be decided was whether the denial of the bad faith claim resulted in American Home waiving privilege in respect of what its counsel did to investigate the claim, and any documents resulting from that investigation. In ordering disclosure, Clackson J. said, at pp. 103-104: Litigation privilege extends to the facts acquired by counsel other than those necessary for pleading. … Litigation privilege does not extend to the actions of counsel. As the actions of American Home's counsel in investigating the claim are relevant to the bad faith aspect of the lawsuit, the Defendant must answer whether its counsel conducted any investigations relating to Sovereign General's claim under the labour and material payment bond and, if it did, what those investigations consisted of. This information need not be provided until the contractual claim has been decided. A bad faith claim does not automatically negate a claim to privilege for all purposes. A simple denial of bad faith does not waive privilege. However, if the Defendant, at any time, makes a positive averment that it acted in good faith and in doing so relied on the investigations conducted by counsel or privileged advice, that positive averment will be taken as a waiver of privilege. (xxv) Communications to facilitate crime In AARC Society v. Sparks, 2018 ABCA 177, 2018 CarswellAlta 901, 71 Alta. L.R. (6th) 83, 19 C.P.C. (8th) 254, the Court explained the exception to privilege which occurs when the communication sought to be protected was intended to facilitate commission of a crime. The Court said: 2 In order for solicitor-client privilege to apply to communications between a lawyer and client, the communications must be made for the legitimate purpose of obtaining lawful legal advice; that is, “lawful professional advice or assistance”: R v Durham Regional Crime Stoppers Inc, 2017 SCC 45 at para 25, [2017] 2 SCR 157. The communication does not have to be in contemplation of litigation, and the privilege is of permanent duration: Blank v Canada (Minister of Justice), 2006 SCC 39 (CanLII) at para 37, [2006] 2 SCR 319. An exception exists when such communications “between a lawyer and client are criminal or else made with a view to obtaining legal advice to facilitate the commission of a crime” (R v Campbell, [1999] 1 SCR 565 at para 55, 171 DLR (4th) 193), or as part of committing a crime (Descôteaux v Mierzwinski, [1982] 1 SCR 860 at 881, 1982 CanLII 22, citing R v Cox and Railton (1884), 14 QBD 153 at 167). The rule does not apply to these communications, because “the protection of such communications cannot possibly be otherwise than injurious to the interests of justice, and to those of the administration of justice”: Descôteaux at 881. (xxvi) Workers' Compensation Act Section 142 of the Workers' Compensation Act, S.A. 1981, c. W-16, says: “The books, records, documents and files of the Board and all reports, statements and other documents filed with the Board or provided to it are privileged and are not admissible in evidence in any action or proceeding without the consent of the Board.” In Jahnke v. Wylie (1994), 26 Alta. L.R. (3d) 46 (C.A.), Kerans J.A. concluded that s. 142 142 did not apply to an action in which the Board was a party. At p. 50 he said: I conclude that actions in which the Board is a party are necessarily outside the scope of the provision. In other words, I would read down “any” in “any action or proceeding” to mean any action other than one in which the Board is a party, and thus give effect to a meaning that, in my view, is necessarily implicit. His Lordship went on to say, at p. 54: I conclude that s. 142 142 forbids a Court from ordering access in any case where the Board is not a party; it instead imposes upon the Board a duty to decide whether to permit disclosure, a duty that must be exercised fairly. (xxvii) Physician/Patient Confidentiality and the Right of “Full and Complete Defence” In Phillip (Next Friend of) v. Whitecourt General Hospital, 2001 CarswellAlta 543, 290 A.R. 228, 92 Alta. L.R. (3d) 321, a medical malpractice action was commenced by a plaintiff who complained of long-term medical problems resulting from inadequate medical care. Counsel for the defendant physicians intended to interview the plaintiff's “treating physicians”, but plaintiff's counsel objected on the basis of physician-patient confidentiality. Murray J. said, at p. 343: Thus, I am satisfied that it is a law of Alberta that the patient's right to confidentiality and privacy is overridden by “the public interest in an efficient administration of justice, including the right to full and complete defence” and the need to protect the integrity of the principles inherent in our adversarial system of justice. …[C]ounsel for the Defendant is at liberty to interview a “treating physician” provided that that physician is prepared to speak to such counsel, having in mind Rule 22 of the Code of Conduct of the Canadian Medical Association and, in the case of counsel, Rule 22 of the Law Society Code of Conduct. The scope of such interview insofar as it relates to the patient is restricted to relevant factual information and if the physician has agreed to give evidence as an expert, it cannot touch upon such information as he has received from his patient's counsel in the context of that designation. There may be other limitations which defence counsel must observe. His Lordship then discussed the procedure to be followed when counsel wishes to interview physicians who have treated the Plaintiff. At pp. 345-346, his Lordship said: The procedures which, in my opinion, should be followed in the future in all cases involving “treating physicians”, whether or not he has yet been consulted as an expert by counsel on behalf of his patient, should be as follows: 1. Once the Affidavit of Records has been filed and any disputes as to relevancy or materiality respecting the “treating physician's” records has been resolved, counsel for the defendant may serve notice upon the patient's counsel that he will be approaching the treating physician to obtain that physician's agreement to being interviewed respecting matters relevant and material to the litigation. 2. Such notice must be reasonable and, in my view, two weeks would be appropriate. 3. A copy of such notice should be sent to the “treating physician” together with a copy of those portions of the medical records disclosed in the Affidavit of Records in such form as that document has been finalized prior to examinations for discovery. The physician's attention should be drawn to any portions of his records which are not considered to be relevant and therefore retain their confidentiality. Accompanying such notice to the “treating physician” should be a copy of the relevant portions of the Code of Conduct of the Canadian Medical Association and advice to the effect that the “treating physician” has no obligation to grant such an interview and may wish to speak to independent legal counsel before agreeing to do so. 4. The onus is upon counsel for the patient to make any application to bar, restrict, or in some way limit such interviews prior to the expiry of the two-week period. This is when the court and counsel will be apprised of any irrelevant and thus confidential information possessed by the physician. Also, if the physician has been approached to fill the role as an expert, then counsel and the court had been apprised of this and the court can direct what areas counsel must avoid discussing with the physician. The court may impose a condition such as having the interview recorded for use by the court should a dispute arise as to the scope of the interview. In brief, the court retains its role as the “gatekeeper”. 5. Should counsel for the patient not take such a step and the “treating physician” agrees to the interview, then without more, it may take place. 6. Should counsel for the patient bring such an application it must be brought forthwith and if not proceeded with promptly, counsel for the defendant can apply to have a date set for the hearing. I appreciate that this deviates from the pure rule that there is no property in a witness, it may impede the adversarial system to some degree, and in the case of an expert it enlarges upon the requirements of rule 22 of the Code of Conduct of the Law Society of Alberta. However, having regard to the complexity of the overall situation, it preserves the right of the defendant to make full answer and defence within the context of our adversarial system of justice and lessens, if not eliminates, the risk of inadvertent breach of confidence and, in the case of an expert physician, possible breach of solicitor-client privilege. It must be noted that this ruling applies only where the witness sought to be interviewed is a “treating physician” of a plaintiff in a legal proceeding. The right of defence counsel or plaintiff's counsel to interview other witnesses, professional, expert, or otherwise, who have a relationship with a plaintiff or defendant will depend on the facts in each case. In Weary v. Ramos, 2005 ABQB 750, 2005 CarswellAlta 1478, 385 A.R. 106, 55 Alta. L.R. (4th) 195, a law firm employed a lawyer (Ramos) to fill in for one of the firm's lawyers who was on maternity leave. When Ramos left the firm before the expiration of the fixed term contract, the law firm sued Ramos for wrongful termination of employment. One of the issues between the parties was the calculation of the damages the plaintiff alleged it had suffered as a result of the actions of the defendant. The defendant contended that files of the law firm would have to be reviewed by the defendant “in order to determine whether her premature departure really caused the Plaintiff any damage”. The plaintiff “took the position that the files were subject to solicitor client privilege and should not be produced even though relevant.” Slatter J., in granting a limited form of access to the files, said, at pp. 202-204: In Descouteaux, supra, the Court stated the substantive rule as follows: It would, I think, be useful for us to formulate this substantive rule, as the judges formerly did with the rule of evidence; it could, in my view, be stated as follows: 1. The confidentiality of communications between solicitor and client may be raised in any circumstances where such communications are likely to be disclosed without the client's consent. 2. Unless the law provides otherwise, when and to the extent that the legitimate exercise of a right would interfere with another person's right to have his communications with his lawyer kept confidential, the resulting conflict should be resolved in favour of protecting the confidentiality. 3. When the law gives someone the authority to do something which, in the circumstances of the case, might interfere with that confidentiality, the decision to do so and the choice of means of exercising that authority should be determined with a view to not interfering with it except to the extent absolutely necessary in order to achieve the ends sought by the enabling legislation. 4. Acts providing otherwise in situations under paragraph 2 and enabling legislation referred to in paragraph 3 must be interpreted restrictively. In this case the first point is admitted. The clients have not been asked to consent to the release of their files. The second and third points are engaged, because the Rules of Court require the Plaintiff to discover all relevant and material documents, and the Defendant has the right to inspect those documents to mount her defence. The third and fourth parts of the substantive rule then require that the right to inspect be as limited as possible to achieve the ends of the Rules. Obviously, a complete prohibition on inspection of the files would be the most effective means of protecting the privilege. However, Descouteaux does not call for a complete prohibition in every case: see Wilder v. Ontario (Securities Commission) (2001), 53 O.R. (3d) 519, ¶ 32-33 (Ont. C.A.). As stated by G. MacKenzie in Lawyers and Ethics (Thomson Carswell), at para. 3.6: The confidentiality rule is for the most part beneficial, and it is essential to the preservation of values that we hold dear. The rule is not absolute; it admits limited exceptions. The real difficulties are, first, that the means of resolving conflicts between confidentiality and other values have not been adequately addressed; second, that the exceptions are inadequate and sometimes self-serving; and third, that the rule does not allow for the various competing interests to be balanced in individual cases, so that the desirability of maintaining confidentiality may be weighed against the desirability of permitting disclosure. Thus both the rule and the exceptions have generally been applied mechanically, with little heed paid to the harm such a ritualistic approach may cause. The substantive rule stated in Descouteaux implies that there will be occasions where the right to privilege will be balanced against competing rights. This is one such case. I prefer the functional approach in Pomer and Lazare to the more rigid approach in Kupferstein and O'Donohue. I have concluded that in this case the Defendant should be granted a limited form of access to the files. This is primarily because of the following factors: (a) All involved in this litigation (including counsel for the parties) are members of the Bar, and are bound to protect the confidentiality of the files. (b) The Defendant was at one time in a solicitor and client relationship with many of the clients, and has already seen the files. (c) There is an implied exception to the privilege rule that allows disclosure of the files in the ordinary course of the lawyer's business, as long as there is a reasonable expectation the privilege will be protected, and this is such an occasion. (d) The documents in question (particularly the real estate files and the accounting records) are unlikely to be highly sensitive (as compared, for example, to criminal files): R. v. Murray (2000), 48 O.R. (3d) 437, ¶ 14 (Ont. S.C.J.). The files should therefor be discovered in this litigation. Conclusion In conclusion, the files and accounting records in question appear to be relevant and material. From time to time law firms become engaged in litigation, and the production of the files is necessary to allow the lawyer to conduct business in the ordinary course. Production of the files in those circumstances is contemplated by the Code of Professional Conduct. Furthermore, the proposed recipient of the information is someone who has already seen the information, or part of it. In all of the circumstances, the files should be produced. That being said, in my view it would be excessive, and contrary to the spirit of Descôteaux, to require the Plaintiff to provide photocopies of all of the files to the Defendant. The Rules of Court give the Defendant the right to inspect the files, but wholesale copying of the files is not called for, and the Defendant is only permitted to take such extracts from the file as are reasonably necessary for the purposes of this litigation. Any dispute over which parts of the files can be copied will have to be resolved by application. In accordance with her responsibilities as a litigant, and also as a member of the Bar, the Defendant and her counsel are not to disclose the contents of the privileged files to any third person. The files are not to be introduced at trial without a prior ruling by the trial judge. (xxviii) Protocol for Dealing with Privileged Documents In 0678786 BC Ltd. v. Bennett Jones LLP, 2021 ABCA 62, 2021 CarswellAlta 339, additional reasons 2021 ABCA 197, leave to appeal refused 2021 CarswellAlta 2491 (S.C.C.), the Court of Appeal discussed situations in which privileged documents come into the hands of third parties: [26] Privileged documents can sometimes come into the hands of third parties. Sometimes that happens as a result of inadvertence: Celanese Canada Inc v Murray Demolition Corp, 2006 SCC 36 at para. 57, [2006] 2 SCR 189. In Celanese Canada, disclosure occurred because of the undisciplined execution of an Anton Piller order. In British Columbia (Attorney General) v Lee, 2017 BCCA 219 at para. 59, 414 DLR (4th) 635 the documents were disclosed as a result of the type of administrative error that is “bound to occur from time to time”. Sometimes disclosure may be the result of “positive misconduct”: Firemaster Oilfield Services Ltd v Safety Boss (Canada) (1993) Ltd, 2000 ABQB 932 at paras. 17, 23, 81 Alta LR (3d) 385, 285 AR 141 affirmed 2001 ABCA 248, 96 Alta LR (3d) 212, 293 AR 366. [27] When a lawyer comes into possession of potentially privileged documents, there is a protocol that has been established. In Firemaster Oilfield at para. 7 the Court of Appeal summarized the rule: 7. … The plain duty of the recipient counsel was to seal them up, not read them further, take no copies, take no notes, and return any copies or notes already taken. At the very highest, the appellant lawyers could have sealed everything up and got the court's direction. This protocol should be observed whenever there is a reasonable prospect that the documents are privileged. Any uncertainty about whether there was a solicitor and client retainer, or whether there has been waiver, should be resolved by the court before the documents are disclosed or used in any way. [28] The Code of Conduct of The Law Society of Alberta states the basic principle, including that the opposing lawyer must be advised of the inadvertent disclosure: Inadvertent Communications
paragraphs.heading: Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 5 (Part 3)

sentences.text: A reasonable reconciliation of these apparently different approaches and cases is that the communication must be part of a correspondence which the parties intend will reasonably lead to a compromise or settlement of the dispute.

Hence, letters designed to open such negotiations, or letters or discussions which attempt to convince the opponent of the strengths of the other's position, but which also recognize weaknesses, in the hope that some settlement can be effected once each other's positions are on the table, should be subject to the privilege, whether or not they contain an actual offer of settlement. . . . . .
There are a few exceptions to the rule that without prejudice correspondence may not be referred to in evidence.
For example, if an application is brought to strike proceedings for want of prosecution, it is possible to explain the delay by indicating that negotiations have been underway.

However, in these circumstances it will seldom be necessary or permissible to actually attach the without prejudice correspondence to an affidavit; it will be sufficient to merely refer to the discussions, and perhaps note the dates of the correspondence back and forth.
There may also be statutory exceptions to this privilege, such as Rule 11.
This Rule provides how long a statement of claim is in effect, how it can be reviewed, and the effects of expiry.

Rule 11(9) provides when a defendant cannot rely on expiry of the statement of claim, and Rule 11(9)(a)(iii) includes as part of the test whether a person “purported to negotiate on behalf of the defendant.” This rule effectively makes negotiations a fact in issue.
Therefore where Rule 11(9)(a)(iii) is relied on (i.e. a standstill agreement is alleged) it may be necessary to refer to correspondence that is clearly privileged.
This should not be taken as a license by counsel to attach all manner of privileged correspondence to affidavits, even when a standstill agreement is alleged.
In most cases an affidavit deposing to negotiations generally, and referring to correspondence back and forth, or perhaps quoting particular sentences, will be sufficient.
In all cases actual sums offered should be blacked out; they are irrelevant and there is a risk they might come to the attention of the trial judge.
Rule 173 prohibits reference to any formal offers.
There is another situation that has nothing to do with settlement at all Correspondence is sometimes marked “without prejudice” other than when it is intended that the settlement privilege attach.
For example, a lawyer might write outlining what he expects his client or another witness would say at trial.
Comments such as this might be made as a form of disclosure, in order to simplify the proceedings.

When they are marked “without prejudice,” that really means “this is not an admission.” Sometimes “without prejudice” is intended to preserve the formal rights of the party, or disclaim responsibility for the contents of the letter.
Other examples are given by D.
Vaver, “Without Prejudice Communications—Their Admissibility and Effect” (1974), 9 U.B.C.
L.
Rev.
Such correspondence is not generally admissible as evidence, not because it is privileged, but because it is hearsay, irrelevant or was not intended to have legal effect.
In Leonardis v.
Leonardis, 2003 ABQB 577, 2003 CarswellAlta 940, 50 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 56, Slatter J. reaffirmed the statements he made in Hansraj v.
Ao, 2002 ABQB 385, 2002 CarswellAlta 627, 314 A.R.
262, 4 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 124; additional reasons at 2002 ABQB 772, 2002 CarswellAlta 1064, 314 A.R.
283, 4 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 147; additional reasons at 2003 ABQB 299, 2003 CarswellAlta 508, 16 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 296, and spoke specifically of the privilege which attaches to settlement correspondence.
At p.
58, his Lordship said: This decision involves the third type of privilege, namely that relating to communications in furtherance of settlement.
There are two important things to note about the settlement privilege.
The first is that the privilege belongs to both parties, and it cannot be unilaterally waived by either one.
Therefore, no party can unilaterally purport to waive privilege and attach such privileged materials to an affidavit or otherwise mention them in court.
The second point is that it is the contents of the communication that determine if it is privileged, not the way it is labelled.
If the contents of a communication are truly in furtherance of settlement and therefore privileged, it makes no difference whether the communication is marked “Without Prejudice” or not.
A communication that is not in substance privileged does not become so just because one party places “Without Prejudice” on it.
Likewise, the absence of the words “Without Prejudice” means nothing if the communication is truly privileged. … Slatter J. discussed the use of the phrase “With Prejudice”, and said at p.
60: There are occasions when it is appropriate to place “With Prejudice” on a letter.
Examples are where the author of the letter seeks to fix legal rights, as where the letter demands payment of a sum, or exercises an option or election, or gives notice of a breach of a contract.
However, placing “With Prejudice” on a settlement offer is inappropriate and ineffective.
Justice Schutz in 1021018 Alberta Ltd. v.
Bazinet, 2015 ABQB 151 explained how a Court should treat communications marked “with prejudice” (at paras 12-22) and applied Slatter J.'s decision in Leonardis v.
Leonardis, 2003 ABQB 577, 2003 CarswellAlta 940, 50 Alta.
L.R.

(xvi) Settlement negotiations It is, of course, well established that communications exchanged in the course of settlement negotiations often satisfy those criteria and accordingly are held to be privileged and inadmissible. . . . . .
As Ruttan J. stated in Knight v.
Ericksson (1958), 26 W.W.R.
C.A.): “To permit evidence of offers made in such a manner to be used against the party making them would be to discourage parties from ever arriving at settlements to compromise litigation”.
Costello v.
Calgary (City) (1997), 53 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 15 C.A., at pp.
45-46, per Picard J.A.
In Bellatrix Exploration Ltd. v.
Penn West Petroleum Ltd., 2013 ABCA 10, 2013 CarswellAlta 76, 542 A.R.
83, 81 Alta.
L.R.

(5th) 84, the Court gave this summary of the law of settlement privilege (at paragraphs 21–31): Purpose and Scope of Settlement Privilege 21 Settlement privilege is premised on the public policy goal of encouraging the settlement of disputes without the need to resort to litigation.
It allows parties to freely discuss and offer terms of settlement in an attempt to reach a compromise.

Because an admission of liability is often implicit as part of settlement negotiations, the rule ensures that communications made in the course of settlement negotiations are generally not admitted into evidence.
Otherwise, parties would rarely, if ever, enter into settlement negotiations to resolve their legal disputes.

22 Other justifications for the rule have been offered, including the notion that an implied contract is created between negotiating parties, such that any admissions made in their discussions will be considered confidential.

While this theory has often been rejected as being problematic and not well-founded, it has received some recent acceptance in the English case law, which was expanded upon by the Newfoundland Court of Appeal in Meyers.
23 Alberta courts have adopted the public policy rationale for the rule: see Ed Miller Sales & Rentals Ltd v.
Caterpillar Tractor Co.
See also Costello at para 94; Hansraj v.
Ao, 2002 ABQB 385, 314 AR 262, rev'd on other grounds 2004 ABCA 223, 354 AR 91.

This approach is consistent with the underlying objective that the parties should be permitted to freely “put all their cards on the table” without having to worry that they may be prejudiced should negotiations fail to resolve their dispute.

24 Courts appear to have accepted that the types of communications covered by the settlement privilege require at least a hint of potential compromise or negotiation: see, for example, Hansraj at para 20.
However, an unconditional assertion of rights without any connection to the possibility of settlement or negotiation do not fall within the scope of the rule: Buckinghamshire County Council v.
Moran, [1990] 1 Ch 623, [1989] 3 All ER 225 (CA), cited in Hansraj at para 19.
Communications of this type do not offer any potential for compromise, which is the interest the privilege is intended to protect.
25 The notation “without prejudice” is not conclusive in establishing privilege.
If the contents of a communication are truly in furtherance of settlement, and therefore privileged, it makes no difference whether the communication is marked “without prejudice” or not.
A communication that is not in substance privileged does not become so just because one party places “without prejudice” on it.
Likewise, the absence of the words “without prejudice” means nothing if the communication is truly privileged: see Leonardis v.
Leonardis, 2003 ABQB 577 at para 6, 50 Alta LR (4th) 56; Phillips v.
Rogers (1988), 92 AR 253, 62 Alta LR (2d) 140 (QB); William Allan Real Estate Co v.
Robichaud (1987), 37 BLR 286, 17 CPC (2d) 138 (Ont HC); Underwood v.
Cox (1912), 21 OWR 757, 26 OLR 303 at 310 (Div Ct); Imperial Oil Ltd. v.
416169 Alberta Inc., 2002 ABQB 386 at para 30, 310 AR 338.
26 As settlement privilege operates to preclude admission of evidence that might otherwise be relevant, it competes with the court's truth-seeking function.
For that reason, courts must ensure the communications come within the tripartite test before applying the privilege.

However, once that test is met, the privilege must be given broad scope and attach not only to communications involving offers of settlement but also to communications that are reasonably connected to the parties' negotiations.
The privilege belongs to both parties and cannot be unilaterally waived or overridden by either of them: see Hansraj at para 13.

27 It is to be remembered that the rationale for the privilege is not limited to the notion that it would be unfair to subsequently prejudice one of the parties by admitting any admissions made during settlement negotiations.

The rule is also intended to allow parties to freely and openly discuss the potential for a settlement, and while doing so, the parties should not have to carefully monitor the content of their discussions.
As noted by Lord Walker in Unilever plc v.
The Procter & Gamble Co.
(1999), [2001] 1 All ER 783 at para 35, [2000] 1 WLR 2436 (CA): the protection of admissions against interest is the most important practical effect of the rule.

But to dissect out identifiable admissions and withhold protection from the rest of without prejudice communications (except for a special reason) would not only create huge practical difficulties but would be contrary to the underlying objective of giving protection to the parties.

28 In other words, the rule's protection is not meant to be limited to the prejudice that an admission may have at trial specifically, but on the potential impairment on settlement discussions as an important element of the litigation process generally.

Accordingly, for the rule to operate properly, not only must the ambit of the settlement privilege be broad, but the exceptions to the exclusionary rule must be narrowly construed and only be given effect where another policy objective can be shown to outweigh any impact that may arise to the settlement objective.
Exceptions to Settlement Privilege 29 As with most forms of privilege, there are exceptions to the rule.
Some are universally accepted, while others are more controversial.
Among the generally recognized exceptions are the following: (a) to prevent double recovery: Dos Santos (Committee of) v.
Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada, 2005 BCCA 4, 207 BCAC 54
(b) where the communications are unlawful, containing for example, threats or fraud
(c) to prove that a settlement (an accord and satisfaction) was reached, or to determine the exact terms of the settlement: Comrie v.
Comrie, 2001 SKCA 33, 203 Sask R 164; (d) it is possible that the settlement posture of the parties can be relevant to costs.
That is clearly the case with offers made under the Rules of Court, but also with respect to informal offers: Mahe v.
Boulianne, 2010 ABCA 74 at paras 8–10, 21 Alta LR (5th) 277; Calderbank v.
Calderbank, [1975] 3 All ER 333 (CA).
30 Some of these may not truly be exceptions to the rule, but simply matters outside the scope of the rule.
For example, using without prejudice communications to prove that a settlement was actually achieved is not inconsistent with the policy behind the privilege.
Similarly, it may be that even if part of a communication is covered by the privilege another part, such as a separate enclosure might not be.
31 The English cases identify some possible exceptions to the privilege, sometimes in very wide terms.

For example, Lord Walker stated in Unilever at para 37: “… the veil imposed by public policy may have to be pulled aside, even so as to disclose admissions, in cases where the protection afforded by the rule has been unequivocally abused.”[emphasis added.] However, courts must proceed cautiously before establishing exceptions to settlement privilege, as the underlying public policy justification is a compelling one: see Brown v.
Cape Breton (Regional Municipality), 2011 NSCA 32 at para 65, 331 DLR (4th) 307.

[22] In general, one can take from General Accident Assurance that the determination of solicitor-client privilege is contextual, fact based and evidence-dependent and the criteria for the existence of privilege is the necessary pre-condition for all determinations, including those that arise from third-party involvement.
