[25] Consequently, and in the context of Gill J's February 13, 2019 Consent Procedural Order, I find that solicitor-client privilege attaches to all of the documents contained in the Sealed Records.
I have reviewed them individually.
(xviii) Continuum of communication In Power v.
RGMP, 2021 ABQB 877, 2021 CarswellAlta 2819, Justice Grosse gave this summary: [16] Solicitor-client privilege is not merely a rule of evidence.
It is recognized as a fundamental principle of substance, as close to absolute as possible: R v McClure, 2001 SCC 14 at paras 2, 5 and 35.

In order for a communication to be protected by solicitor-client privilege, it must: (a) Be made between a lawyer and a client; (b) Entail seeking or providing legal advice; and (c) Be intended by the lawyer and client to be confidential.
Canada v Solosky, 1979 CanLII 9 (SCC), [1980] 1 SCR 821 at 837.
[17] Although not all communications between legal counsel and a client are privileged, the Court does not engage in a line by line review to identify “advice”.
A “continuum of communications” between lawyer and client is necessary in order for the lawyer to understand the client's circumstances and advise accordingly.

Communications are protected if they fall within that continuum, even if that particular communication does not itself specifically include advice or a request for advice: Blood Tribe v Canada (Attorney General), 2010 ABCA 112 at para 26.
This is consistent with one of the underlying premises of solicitor-client privilege, being the need for clients and lawyers to be able to communicate freely and candidly: McClure at para 2.
Undue parsing would thwart this objective.

Where a corporation is the client, communications within the corporation for the purposes of discussing a request for advice, or advice received, or otherwise to obtain advice and instruct counsel, may be subject to solicitor-client privilege: Bank of Montreal v Tortora, 2010 BCSC 1430 at para 12.

[18] Whether a particular communication is privileged is contextual and must be decided based on the evidence in the case before the court: General Accident Assurance Co v Chrusz, 1999 CanLII 7320 (ON CA), 1999 CarswellOnt 2898 at paras 95-96, per Doherty JA, dissenting on other points.
The party asserting a privilege bears the onus of establishing the privilege: Alberta (Provincial Treasurer) v Pocklington Foods Inc, 1993 ABCA 69; 1993 CarswellAlta 312 at para 42.
The Court may infer that some elements of the test are met, without specific evidence: Blood Tribe at para 19.

For example, if a communication is clearly between a lawyer and client for the purpose of giving or receiving legal advice, and there is no evidence that it was shared with any third party, an inference is readily available that the communication was intended to be confidential.
C. — Common Interest Privilege [19] Many of the records in dispute are not communications between one party and their counsel.
Rather, they are communications between CanAm and RGMP, or between their respective transaction counsel, or some combination of parties and counsel.
In cases where the communication is not between counsel and client, CanAm and RGMP argue that the records are subject to “common interest privilege”.
They describe the communications as being “in furtherance of the transaction” or “for the purposes of completing the offering” or similar descriptions.
[20]“Common interest privilege” is not a stand-alone privilege.
Common interest privilege only protects records that are otherwise protected by another privilege.

In fact, it is frequently suggested that common interest privilege is not a privilege at all, but rather, an exception to the doctrine of waiver: Piney Bowes of Canada Ltd v R, 2003 FTC 214 at para 14
A Dodek, Solicitor-Client Privilege (LexisNexis Canada Inc, 2014) at § 7.162.

Because confidentiality is an essential element of solicitor-client privilege, if a party knowingly shares communication that would otherwise meet the test for solicitor-client privilege with a third party, the privilege is often waived: see the summary of waiver in Dodek, supra at § 7.4.

Common interest privilege acknowledges that in some circumstances, the holder of the privilege and the third party may have sufficient common interest in the subject matter of the privileged communication, including an interest in maintaining confidence, that disclosure to the third party does not interfere with the communication's privileged status.

[21]“Common interest privilege” was originally recognized in the context of parties with a common interest in the subject matter of anticipated litigation sharing advice or documents: Buttes Gas and Oil Co v Hammer (No 3), [1980] All ER 475 (Eng CA), varied [1982] AC 888 (HL).
It has been applied to both communication subject to solicitor-client privilege and to information subject to litigation privilege.

For the purposes of this decision, I need not address the distinctions between those two privileges and their underpinnings, and how those distinctions impact the application of “common interest privilege”: see Pinder v Sproule, 2003 ABQB 33 at paras 54, 62.
It is important that a party claiming “common interest privilege” articulate the basis on which the record is privileged and how the “common interest privilege” applies to that particular record.
[22] I note at this juncture that common interest privilege is not to be confused with joint client privilege.
The latter applies where two parties retain the same counsel, or in other circumstances where the advice is deemed to be sought for the joint benefit of more than one party: Dodek, supra at § 2.4.
There is no claim of joint client privilege here.
[23] Common interest privilege has now expanded beyond the context of litigation or anticipated litigation.

Canadian law recognizes that parties to a transaction may enjoy common interest privilege.[2] In Iggillis Holdings Inc v Canada (Minister of National Revenue), the Federal Court of Appeal described common interest privilege in the transaction context as follows: “… solicitor-client privilege is not waived when an opinion provided by a lawyer to one party is disclosed, on a confidential basis, to other parties with sufficient common interest in the same transactions”: Iggillis Holdings Inc v Canada (Minister of National Revenue), 2018 FCA 51 at para 41; leave to appeal dismissed [2018] SCCA No 207 (QL).

[24] Most of the commonly cited cases on common interest privilege in a transaction context involve substantive legal opinions shared by parties to a transaction, often on a specific legal point, such as foreign law or tax: for example, see Archean Energy Ltd v Minister of National Revenue, 1997 CarswellAlta 247 at para 30
Fraser Milner Casgrain LLP v Minister of National Resources, 2002 BCSC 1344
Pitney Bowes of Canada Ltd v R, 2003 FCT 214
Iggillis, supra.

Another confirmed example is disclosure of privileged records so as to permit the counterparty to do due diligence on the underlying subject matter: Anderson Exploration Ltd v Pan-Alberta Gas Ltd, 1998 ABQB 455. … [35] In considering the application of solicitor-client privilege and common interest privilege in this context, I see a distinction between a party conveying a position, or making a request or demand of the other party, and sharing legal advice.
To take a general example, not at issue in this particular case, counsel may provide advice to a client that a certain form of indemnity would be in the client's best interest.
Such advice is prima facie subject to solicitor-client privilege.

However, if the client accepts that advice, and, in the course of negotiations with the counterparty, requests the inclusion of that indemnity, the request to the counter-party is not likely to be treated as sharing solicitor-client privileged information.
The same is true whether the request for the indemnity is conveyed by the client or by counsel.
Without more, the request for the indemnity is more akin to a statement of position, or a volley in the negotiations, than to a sharing of privileged legal advice.

If all such communications were protected under the umbrella of solicitor-client privilege and common interest privilege, just because they were based on legal advice, or because counsel was involved in the communication, it would amount, in effect, to the creation of a stand-alone transactional privilege for any deals involving counsel.
No such privilege has ever been recognized.
CanAm and RGMP do not expressly argue for any such recognition, but it would be the natural extension of their position.
[36] Of course, the line may not always be clear, and each case turns on its own facts and record.

A series of similar communication could be found to be privileged in one case, and not in another, either because of differing surrounding circumstances, different specific content, different specificity of evidence before the court, or a myriad of other factors.
My reasons herein should not be taken as trying to draw hard and fast rules about certain types of records or patterns of communications in the context of every commercial transaction.

[37] General descriptions of types of records that I have concluded are not privileged in the Production Application include: • Emails between counsel requesting or providing status updates. • Emails directly between counsel for one party and representatives of the other party requesting or providing factual information. • Communications between the parties discussing tasks to be completed and requesting or providing factual information.

In my view, an exchange as to who each party is retaining as counsel falls within this category and is not privileged, even where counsel is introduced by copying them. • Internal communications amongst CanAm personnel, not involving CanAm counsel, relating to gathering information to respond to a request for information from RGMP or RGMP's counsel.
The face of the communications, context and evidentiary record do not establish that these are part of the continuum of communications for giving or receiving legal advice.
[38] The issue with respect to the above records is not whether there was waiver saved by common interest privilege.
Rather, they are not protected by solicitor-client privilege in the first place.

They are communications between the parties or their counsel that do not amount to sharing of legal advice. … With respect to draft documents, Her Ladyship said: [41] As a starting proposition, I accept that in preparing a draft agreement, in commenting on a draft, or in proposing revisions to a draft, a lawyer usually brings to bear their legal experience and expertise.

Accordingly, when the draft, comments or proposed revisions are communicated to the lawyer's client, they are usually subject to solicitor-client privilege.[4] [42] In a broad sense, all communications between counterparties or their counsel on drafts could be said to be made in confidence, and in furtherance of a common interest in improving and finalizing the transaction agreements.

To pick up on the words of Justice O'Reilly in Pitney Bowes, these communications could allow the parties to have an appreciation of the legal position of the others, as provided by a respected solicitor, allowing negotiations to proceed in an informed and open way: Pitney Bowes at para 20.

However, unless the record itself, context and/or evidence demonstrate otherwise, these exchanges, even if collaborative in tone, are usually more akin to a statement of position, or otherwise “adversarial” communications wherein each party tries to achieve the best possible deal for itself: Pitney Bowes at para 19.
They are not privileged, even though the position may be based on, or even the same as, the legal advice communicated between the sending party and their own counsel.
[43] Three particular draft/comment scenarios in the disputed records warrant a more robust explanation to the parties than I can practically fit in the Chart.
The first is where counsel provided a draft or comments to their client on transaction documents, and then the client forwarded that communication to the other party or their counsel.

Even accepting that the underlying draft or comments were subject to solicitor-client privilege between counsel and client, without an evidentiary and/or contextual basis establishing that the forwarding was a sharing of legal advice in confidence, I find that the proper characterization of the forwarding communication is a statement of position to the other party.
In essence, the party has adopted the lawyer's advice and it has become their position.
That the party chose to simply forward the lawyer's correspondence or work product instead of preparing their own communication based on the legal advice does not change the result.
To the extent the underlying, forwarded communications are in issue, a waiver analysis applies.
The reasonable inference in the circumstances before me is that privilege was waived by way of intentional disclosure of the privileged communication to the opposing party.
There is no suggestion of inadvertent disclosure or that the forwarding party was unaware of the privilege.
The Defendants have not established that the disclosure was in furtherance of a common interest or to promote a common understanding on a particular point.
Rather, the disclosure was simply a convenient way of communicating the party's position.

[44] The second variation involves counsel sending their draft, comments or revisions on transaction documents to the opposing party and/or opposing counsel concurrently with sending them to their own client for review.
Again, this type of correspondence could reflect counsel providing or sharing legal advice for the benefit of the group to advance and improve the transaction documents for all.
However, there has to be a basis in the documents themselves, the context and/or the evidence to support that characterization; there is no such basis here.
The correspondence is simply counsel communicating a preliminary or conditional position on behalf of the client.
This is so even though the same communication sent only to the client would be prima facie privileged.
Between lawyer and client only, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, the readily available inference is that the draft or comments are confidential advice.

The same inference is not available where the communication includes the counterparty. … [48]… However, as set out above, not every disclosure of privileged communication with another party to a transaction is automatically covered by common interest privilege.

In fact, the starting point for communication between counsel for independent parties to a transaction would be that it is not privileged and that to the extent it discloses otherwise privileged information, the privilege is waived.

Counsel are expected to understand privilege and waiver, and they may waive on behalf of a client. …[49] The onus is on CanAm and RGMP to establish, by way of the records themselves, the context and/or evidence, that the draft financing statement, and advice related to it, were communicated between them as a sharing of legal advice in confidence, as opposed to some other purpose, and that they had a common interest in respect of that advice sufficient to warrant protection by common interest privilege. … As to the burden on the party claiming the privilege, Her Ladyship said: [53] I have considered whether my findings above ask too much of RGMP and CanAm.
I am not convinced they do.
There is no class privilege for transaction communications, whether between parties or counsel.
There is no blanket common interest privilege over privileged communications disclosed in the context of a transaction.
Solicitor-client privilege is a principle of substance and should be carefully guarded.

Even in the context of a time-sensitive transaction, where parties and counsel may be pulled in many directions, any disclosure of solicitor-client communication should be thoughtfully considered, with a clear understanding of why the privileged communication is being disclosed and on what basis.

If the disclosure is intended to be made in confidence, pursuant to a common interest without waiving privilege, then the parties should at the time have a reasonable basis for expecting confidentiality, and an ability to articulate the common interest they share in respect of the disclosure of the privileged communication.
As such, later delineating and justifying the claim of common interest privilege should not create an undue hardship.
See also: Justice Dilts' discussion of solicitor-client privilege as it applies to strands of communication between lawyer and client in CNOOC Petroleum North America ULC v.
801 Seventh Inc., 2021 ABQB 861, 2021 CarswellAlta 2725 at paragraphs 28-38.

Once the waiver doctrine is re-evaluated in the manner described above it will become apparent that legal professional privilege is not an absolute rule which may never be derogated from.

While sometimes referred to as instances of “implied intent to waive”, in the absence of any actual intention these factors are more helpfully described as circumstances where by operation of law the privilege is regarded as having been lost.

However, since so many of the cases use the term “waiver” in the broad sense, this annotation will, for purposes of convenience, use the term in that broad sense to cover cases of both actual waiver of privilege and loss of privilege.
Regardless, the distinction between “waiver” and “loss” is conceptually important.
The dominant test for waiver is fairness (although intent is also at its foundation).
Waiver, however, depends upon intention.
The giving of a privileged document to one party in litigation does not necessarily show an intention to waive the privilege in respect of all other parties or in respect of other litigation.
Nor does the failure to object when a privileged document is produced by another party amount to presumed waiver. . . . . .
A close review of the many authorities cited regarding waiver reveals that intention and fairness are at its foundation.
A party who raises in a pleading or in evidence legal advice otherwise privileged cannot assert that privilege against the other party to whom the pleading or evidence is directed.
Intent to waive privilege is implied.
There are cases where disclosure of privileged material was inadvertent, but in those cases, waiver was required because fairness demanded it.
Indeed it is likely that fairness has become the dominant test for waiver rather than intention.

The doctrine of waiver is a narrow one because of the importance of solicitor-client confidences.

When it is suggested that the privilege has been waived, the question becomes whether the event said to be a waiver has made the rationale for the privilege inapplicable, or whether the event otherwise justifies a reversal of the priority. . . . . .

In the context of waiver of solicitor-client privilege, communication of the privileged information to an adversary signals that it is no longer essential to the maintenance of the solicitor client relationship that the confidentiality of the information be preserved.
Alternatively, the privilege might not be upheld if, in the circumstances, the communication of the information makes it unfair to continue to maintain the privilege.

(xxi) When can the privilege be set aside?

Once solicitor-client privilege is established (i.e., the communication was in fact confidential, in the context of a professional relationship and in the course of seeking advice), the categorical circumstances in which disclosure of privileged information by a person other than the client will be permitted are very limited.
Communications which are criminal or which seek to facilitate criminal activities are exempted: [Solosky v.
Canada, [1980] 1 S.C.R.
Similarly, privilege may be set aside when the safety of the public is at risk from nondisclosure of the communications: Jones v.
Smith, [1999] 1 S.C.R.

In addition, the continued existence of solicitor-client privilege is not required where the client no longer has an interest to protect and where nondisclosure would compromise the ability of an accused to defend himself: Smith.

Finally, while the duty of confidentiality survives the death of the client, the privilege enures to the client's successor in title (e.g., heirs) and may be waived by a successor in interest to the client: Goodman Estate v.

(xxvii) Physician/Patient Confidentiality and the Right of “Full and Complete Defence” In Phillip (Next Friend of) v.
Whitecourt General Hospital, 2001 CarswellAlta 543, 290 A.R.
L.R.
(3d) 321, a medical malpractice action was commenced by a plaintiff who complained of long-term medical problems resulting from inadequate medical care.
Counsel for the defendant physicians intended to interview the plaintiff's “treating physicians”, but plaintiff's counsel objected on the basis of physician-patient confidentiality.
Murray J. said, at p.

343: Thus, I am satisfied that it is a law of Alberta that the patient's right to confidentiality and privacy is overridden by “the public interest in an efficient administration of justice, including the right to full and complete defence” and the need to protect the integrity of the principles inherent in our adversarial system of justice. …[C]ounsel for the Defendant is at liberty to interview a “treating physician” provided that that physician is prepared to speak to such counsel, having in mind Rule 22 of the Code of Conduct of the Canadian Medical Association and, in the case of counsel, Rule 22 of the Law Society Code of Conduct.

The scope of such interview insofar as it relates to the patient is restricted to relevant factual information and if the physician has agreed to give evidence as an expert, it cannot touch upon such information as he has received from his patient's counsel in the context of that designation.
There may be other limitations which defence counsel must observe.
His Lordship then discussed the procedure to be followed when counsel wishes to interview physicians who have treated the Plaintiff.
At pp.

345-346, his Lordship said: The procedures which, in my opinion, should be followed in the future in all cases involving “treating physicians”, whether or not he has yet been consulted as an expert by counsel on behalf of his patient, should be as follows: 1.

Once the Affidavit of Records has been filed and any disputes as to relevancy or materiality respecting the “treating physician's” records has been resolved, counsel for the defendant may serve notice upon the patient's counsel that he will be approaching the treating physician to obtain that physician's agreement to being interviewed respecting matters relevant and material to the litigation.
Such notice must be reasonable and, in my view, two weeks would be appropriate.

A copy of such notice should be sent to the “treating physician” together with a copy of those portions of the medical records disclosed in the Affidavit of Records in such form as that document has been finalized prior to examinations for discovery.
The physician's attention should be drawn to any portions of his records which are not considered to be relevant and therefore retain their confidentiality.

Accompanying such notice to the “treating physician” should be a copy of the relevant portions of the Code of Conduct of the Canadian Medical Association and advice to the effect that the “treating physician” has no obligation to grant such an interview and may wish to speak to independent legal counsel before agreeing to do so.
The onus is upon counsel for the patient to make any application to bar, restrict, or in some way limit such interviews prior to the expiry of the two-week period.
This is when the court and counsel will be apprised of any irrelevant and thus confidential information possessed by the physician.

Also, if the physician has been approached to fill the role as an expert, then counsel and the court had been apprised of this and the court can direct what areas counsel must avoid discussing with the physician.
The court may impose a condition such as having the interview recorded for use by the court should a dispute arise as to the scope of the interview.
In brief, the court retains its role as the “gatekeeper”.
Should counsel for the patient not take such a step and the “treating physician” agrees to the interview, then without more, it may take place.
Should counsel for the patient bring such an application it must be brought forthwith and if not proceeded with promptly, counsel for the defendant can apply to have a date set for the hearing.

I appreciate that this deviates from the pure rule that there is no property in a witness, it may impede the adversarial system to some degree, and in the case of an expert it enlarges upon the requirements of rule 22 of the Code of Conduct of the Law Society of Alberta.

However, having regard to the complexity of the overall situation, it preserves the right of the defendant to make full answer and defence within the context of our adversarial system of justice and lessens, if not eliminates, the risk of inadvertent breach of confidence and, in the case of an expert physician, possible breach of solicitor-client privilege.
It must be noted that this ruling applies only where the witness sought to be interviewed is a “treating physician” of a plaintiff in a legal proceeding.

The right of defence counsel or plaintiff's counsel to interview other witnesses, professional, expert, or otherwise, who have a relationship with a plaintiff or defendant will depend on the facts in each case.
In Weary v.
Ramos, 2005 ABQB 750, 2005 CarswellAlta 1478, 385 A.R.
L.R.
(4th) 195, a law firm employed a lawyer (Ramos) to fill in for one of the firm's lawyers who was on maternity leave.
When Ramos left the firm before the expiration of the fixed term contract, the law firm sued Ramos for wrongful termination of employment.
One of the issues between the parties was the calculation of the damages the plaintiff alleged it had suffered as a result of the actions of the defendant.
The defendant contended that files of the law firm would have to be reviewed by the defendant “in order to determine whether her premature departure really caused the Plaintiff any damage”.

The plaintiff “took the position that the files were subject to solicitor client privilege and should not be produced even though relevant.” Slatter J., in granting a limited form of access to the files, said, at pp.

202-204: In Descouteaux, supra, the Court stated the substantive rule as follows: It would, I think, be useful for us to formulate this substantive rule, as the judges formerly did with the rule of evidence; it could, in my view, be stated as follows: 1.
The confidentiality of communications between solicitor and client may be raised in any circumstances where such communications are likely to be disclosed without the client's consent.

Unless the law provides otherwise, when and to the extent that the legitimate exercise of a right would interfere with another person's right to have his communications with his lawyer kept confidential, the resulting conflict should be resolved in favour of protecting the confidentiality.

When the law gives someone the authority to do something which, in the circumstances of the case, might interfere with that confidentiality, the decision to do so and the choice of means of exercising that authority should be determined with a view to not interfering with it except to the extent absolutely necessary in order to achieve the ends sought by the enabling legislation.
Acts providing otherwise in situations under paragraph 2 and enabling legislation referred to in paragraph 3 must be interpreted restrictively.
In this case the first point is admitted.
The clients have not been asked to consent to the release of their files.

The second and third points are engaged, because the Rules of Court require the Plaintiff to discover all relevant and material documents, and the Defendant has the right to inspect those documents to mount her defence.
The third and fourth parts of the substantive rule then require that the right to inspect be as limited as possible to achieve the ends of the Rules.
Obviously, a complete prohibition on inspection of the files would be the most effective means of protecting the privilege.
However, Descouteaux does not call for a complete prohibition in every case: see Wilder v.
Ontario (Securities Commission) (2001), 53 O.R.
As stated by G.
MacKenzie in Lawyers and Ethics (Thomson Carswell), at para.
3.6: The confidentiality rule is for the most part beneficial, and it is essential to the preservation of values that we hold dear.
The rule is not absolute; it admits limited exceptions.

The real difficulties are, first, that the means of resolving conflicts between confidentiality and other values have not been adequately addressed; second, that the exceptions are inadequate and sometimes self-serving; and third, that the rule does not allow for the various competing interests to be balanced in individual cases, so that the desirability of maintaining confidentiality may be weighed against the desirability of permitting disclosure.
Thus both the rule and the exceptions have generally been applied mechanically, with little heed paid to the harm such a ritualistic approach may cause.
The substantive rule stated in Descouteaux implies that there will be occasions where the right to privilege will be balanced against competing rights.
This is one such case.
I prefer the functional approach in Pomer and Lazare to the more rigid approach in Kupferstein and O'Donohue.
I have concluded that in this case the Defendant should be granted a limited form of access to the files.

This is primarily because of the following factors: (a) All involved in this litigation (including counsel for the parties) are members of the Bar, and are bound to protect the confidentiality of the files.
(b) The Defendant was at one time in a solicitor and client relationship with many of the clients, and has already seen the files.

(c) There is an implied exception to the privilege rule that allows disclosure of the files in the ordinary course of the lawyer's business, as long as there is a reasonable expectation the privilege will be protected, and this is such an occasion.
(d) The documents in question (particularly the real estate files and the accounting records) are unlikely to be highly sensitive (as compared, for example, to criminal files): R. v.
Murray (2000), 48 O.R.
The files should therefor be discovered in this litigation.
Conclusion In conclusion, the files and accounting records in question appear to be relevant and material.
From time to time law firms become engaged in litigation, and the production of the files is necessary to allow the lawyer to conduct business in the ordinary course.
Production of the files in those circumstances is contemplated by the Code of Professional Conduct.
Furthermore, the proposed recipient of the information is someone who has already seen the information, or part of it.
In all of the circumstances, the files should be produced.
That being said, in my view it would be excessive, and contrary to the spirit of Descôteaux, to require the Plaintiff to provide photocopies of all of the files to the Defendant.

The Rules of Court give the Defendant the right to inspect the files, but wholesale copying of the files is not called for, and the Defendant is only permitted to take such extracts from the file as are reasonably necessary for the purposes of this litigation.
Any dispute over which parts of the files can be copied will have to be resolved by application.
In accordance with her responsibilities as a litigant, and also as a member of the Bar, the Defendant and her counsel are not to disclose the contents of the privileged files to any third person.
The files are not to be introduced at trial without a prior ruling by the trial judge.

Sometimes that happens as a result of inadvertence: Celanese Canada Inc v Murray Demolition Corp, 2006 SCC 36 at para.
In Celanese Canada, disclosure occurred because of the undisciplined execution of an Anton Piller order.
In British Columbia (Attorney General) v Lee, 2017 BCCA 219 at para.
59, 414 DLR (4th) 635 the documents were disclosed as a result of the type of administrative error that is “bound to occur from time to time”.
Sometimes disclosure may be the result of “positive misconduct”: Firemaster Oilfield Services Ltd v Safety Boss (Canada) (1993) Ltd, 2000 ABQB 932 at paras.
17, 23, 81 Alta LR (3d) 385, 285 AR 141 affirmed 2001 ABCA 248, 96 Alta LR (3d) 212, 293 AR 366.

In Firemaster Oilfield at para.

7 the Court of Appeal summarized the rule: 7. … The plain duty of the recipient counsel was to seal them up, not read them further, take no copies, take no notes, and return any copies or notes already taken.
At the very highest, the appellant lawyers could have sealed everything up and got the court's direction.
This protocol should be observed whenever there is a reasonable prospect that the documents are privileged.
Any uncertainty about whether there was a solicitor and client retainer, or whether there has been waiver, should be resolved by the court before the documents are disclosed or used in any way.
